chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Abdullah ibn al-Dahqan, from Durust ibn Abu Mansur, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The one who does a favor similar to what was done to him has merely repaid it equally; and the one who increases it is grateful, and the one who is grateful is generous.'
And the one who knows that the favor he does is for his own sake will not resent people for their gratitude, nor will he expect them to increase in love for him.
So do not seek thanks from others for what you did for your own sake, which protected your dignity.
And know that the one who seeks a need from you has not spared your face (by keeping his dignity intact while asking), so honor your face by not turning him away empty-handed.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.شَكُوراً: Grateful (in the context of increasing the favor)
key_terms.لَمْ يَسْتَبْطِ: He did not resent/consider it burdensome

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic etiquette for giving favors and receiving gratitude according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This narration, transmitted through the chain of Zurarah to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), highlights the spiritual etiquette of *ihsan* (excellence in giving) by distinguishing between mere reciprocity and superior generosity (*shukran*). It emphasizes that the giver should not seek validation from others, as the true beneficiary of the favor is the giver’s own soul and dignity. The hadith concludes with a practical social guideline to honor the petitioner’s face, reflecting the Shia emphasis on preserving the honor of those who seek one's help.
